title: What makes a good question?
text:
Two phases


Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4)
Scaffolded mini-project:
“Is UK biomass electricity carbon-neutral?”
Real data. Real ambiguity. Culminates in a peer-reviewed policy briefing — with a twist.


Phase 2 (Weeks 5–10)
Your investigation:
Choose a sustainable energy question. Design the study. Analyse the data. Write a 4-page policy report.
This is your summative assessment (30%).




Phase 1 is formative — low stakes, high learning. Everyone works with the same data so you can compare notes.
Phase 2 is summative — you choose the question. Same skills, your topic. Groups of 3–4.
The “twist” in Phase 1: don’t reveal yet. Just say “there’s a twist in Week 4 — you’ll see.”

title: What makes a good question?
text:
What you already know
You’ve done GEOL1151 — you can code in Python, use Jupyter, work with data.

This module uses R instead of Python.


Why? R is built for statistics. The syntax is different, but the ideas are identical. You’ve done pre-term preparation to bridge the gap.


Reassure: if you’ve done the pre-term preparation, you’re ready. If you haven’t, the application session is your safety net.
R and Python have similar philosophies - they are distinct tools, best for different tasks. Knowing a little of both gives you the freedom to choose the best tool for a task.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
What is science?

Not a body of facts
A process for reducing uncertainty
We never prove anything — we accumulate evidence



[20 min block] This is the intellectual foundation for the course.
Start here: science isn’t what you know, it’s how you decide what to believe. Every claim in this module will be held to this standard.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
The cycle





flowchart LR
    A[Observation] --> B[Question]
    B --> C[Hypothesis]
    C --> D[Prediction]
    D --> E[Test]
    E --> F[Revise]
    F --> B
    style A fill:#2471a3,color:#fff
    style E fill:#c0392b,color:#fff






Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Prediction → Test → Revise




Drax power station. © Drax




Walk through each step with a concrete example. The biomass question will serve as our running case study.
Emphasise the cycle — science doesn’t end at “test.” The revision step generates new questions.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Two directions of reasoning


Deductive
General → Specific
If plate tectonics is correct, then we predict matching fossils on separated continents.
We test the prediction.


Inductive
Specific → General
We observe matching fossils on separated continents. We infer the continents were once joined.
We build toward a theory.




USGS, public domain





Both are legitimate but different. Deduction is stronger logically (if the premise is true, the conclusion must follow). Induction is how we actually discover most things.
In practice, science uses both — we inductively form hypotheses, then deductively test them.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Wegener’s continental drift



1912: Alfred Wegener proposes continents move
Right conclusion (they do move)
Wrong mechanism (he proposed centrifugal force)
Decades of resistance — then plate tectonics


The lesson: good science can survive a wrong mechanism. What matters is whether the evidence accumulates.





USGS, public domain





Wegener was a meteorologist, not a geologist — the establishment resisted partly for that reason. Good reminder that the source of an idea doesn’t determine its validity.
The mechanism was eventually supplied by Hess (seafloor spreading) and Wilson (plates).

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Instructions
I’ll show you some statements.
For each one, decide: Is this a testable hypothesis?
Think for 30 seconds, then discuss with your neighbour.


[10 min] Think-pair-share format. Show each statement, pause, then take a few responses.
The biomass statement should produce disagreement — that’s the hook for the rest of the module.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “The Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old”
text:
“The Earth is approximately 4.5 billion years old”

Testable — and extensively tested (radiometric dating, meteorite ages, lunar samples). One of the best-constrained numbers in geoscience.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
“Earthquakes are caused by divine punishment”

Not testable as stated — no observable prediction that distinguishes this from natural causes.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “Wind turbines cause headaches in nearby residents”
text:
“Wind turbines cause headaches in nearby residents”

Testable — but tricky. How do you control for the nocebo effect? Awareness bias? The design of the study matters enormously.


This foreshadows Week 5 (experimental design, confounding).
Don’t resolve it — just flag the complexity.
Introduce the “Dawkins Zone”: Dawkins would like every hypothesis to be scientifically testable. But some might be testable in principle, but not in practice - need impossibly large sample size to detect small effects; or effect may be swamped by confounders.

title: What makes a good question?
section: “CO₂ emissions from burning biomass should be counted as zero”
text:
“CO₂ emissions from burning biomass should be counted as zero”

Testable? It depends.

What timescale?
What system boundary?
“Carbon-neutral” is partly a scientific claim and partly a policy choice.




This is the question that will drive the next four weeks.



This statement should generate genuine disagreement. Some students will say “it depends on the trees regrowing” — good. Others may say “it’s a policy definition, not a scientific hypothesis” — also good.
Don’t resolve it. Leave it open. Curiosity is the goal.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Popper’s insight

We can never prove a theory.
We can only fail to disprove it.


Every test that could have disproven our hypothesis but didn’t makes us a little more confident — but never certain.


[20 min block] This is the philosophical core.
Karl Popper (1934): the demarcation problem. What separates science from non-science? Falsifiability.
You don’t need to go deep into philosophy of science. The practical lesson: seek evidence that could prove you wrong.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Confirmation bias
We naturally seek evidence for what we already believe.

This is not a character flaw — it’s how human cognition works.


Science is a set of tools for overcoming this tendency.


Give an everyday example: you think it always rains on bank holidays. You remember the rainy ones, forget the sunny ones. That’s confirmation bias.
In data analysis: if you only look for patterns that support your hypothesis, you will always find them. This is exactly what Week 4’s “traitor” exercise is about.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
The Wason selection task
Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other.
Rule: “If a card shows a vowel, then the other side has an even number.”


A


K


4


7


Which cards must you turn over to test the rule?


[15 min including exercise] Let students think for 60 seconds, discuss in pairs, then poll via Poll Everywhere.
Most students pick A and 4 (confirmation). The correct answer is A and 7 (seeking disconfirmation).

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Cast your vote










PollEv.com/geol
text geol to 07480 781235

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Why A and 7?


A ✓


K


4


7 ✓



A (vowel): if the other side is odd, the rule is broken
7 (odd): if the other side is a vowel, the rule is broken



K (consonant): the rule says nothing about consonants
4 (even): whether the other side is a vowel or not, nothing is disproved



The key: 4 feels relevant because it confirms the rule. But confirmation doesn’t test anything. Only disconfirmation does.
Link forward: “Hypothesis testing in statistics is a formalised version of this — we ask: if the null hypothesis were true, would we see data this extreme? We’re seeking disconfirmation.”

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Why is this hard?
Humans are wired to confirm, not disconfirm.

In this module, you’ll learn to:

Ask “what evidence would change my mind?”
Seek comparisons, not just supporting cases
Treat uncertainty as information, not failure



This connects to every subsequent week. Week 3: “what assumptions are we making?” Week 6: “how plausible was this before we tested?” Week 8: “what is the model not capturing?”
The habits are the real learning outcome. The specific tests and methods are tools in service of these habits.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Why R?


You know Python (NumPy, Jupyter, pandas)
Same ideas. Different syntax.


R is built for statistics

t.test(), lm(), aov() — one line each
ggplot2 — the grammar of graphics
Built-in data manipulation




You’ll see why this matters starting in Week 2.


[15 min] This is NOT an R lesson. That was pre-work.
The goal: show that R is working, connect it to what they know, and move on. Keep it to ≤10 minutes of live coding.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Live demo










R runs in the browser, on this slide. No switching windows.
elec is already loaded by the starter code. Build from there: elec$bioenergy_twh, bio <- elec$bioenergy_twh, summary(bio), plot(elec$year, bio).
Narrate: “You already know how to do this. head() is like df.head() in pandas. plot() is like plt.plot(). The syntax is different but the logic is identical.”
Make sure something goes wrong, to normalise errors: “This happens to everyone. R’s error messages are actually quite helpful once you learn to read them.” Typing elec$bio is a good one — R partial-matches, so it works, which is its own lesson.
The editor swallows arrow keys and space, so slide navigation needs a click outside the cell first.
≤10 minutes. Then back to slides.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
The setup
The UK burns millions of tonnes of imported wood pellets for electricity.

Most come from forests in the southeastern United States.








Figure 1






w01-pellet-origins.R



Little aside: I’m going to try to hold myself to the same standards of data presentation to which you should aspire. It’s your job to call out when I make a claim that’s not supported by the evidence I am presenting.
Here’s a first (pedantic?) example: The chart records country of origin, not region: “southeastern” is from the sourcing literature, not from this data. The claim on the slide is finer-grained than the evidence behind it.
“Millions of tonnes” is now a number they can read off. Plant the seed: is 9.3 Mt a big number? That question is next week’s.




Under international carbon accounting rules, the CO₂ released at the chimney is counted as zero.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Is that reasonable?

Work in pairs. You have 10 minutes.


Write one testable hypothesis about biomass energy
What data would you need to test it?
What evidence would disprove your hypothesis?



[20 min] Circulate and listen. Collect a few examples on the board / shared doc.
Good hypotheses might be: “Biomass electricity produces less CO₂ per kWh than coal” (testable, but depends on system boundary). “Transporting pellets from the US adds significant emissions” (testable with import data + transport factors).
The disprove question is the hard one — and the most valuable. It forces students to think like Popper.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
What you came up with

Click into the box before typing: while it has focus, space and the arrow keys go into the text rather than advancing the slide. Click outside (or press Esc) to get navigation back.

If anyone says “it depends on the timescale” or “it depends on what you include” — celebrate this. That’s exactly right, and it’s what Week 3 is about.
End the session with the question feeling genuinely open. Resist giving the punchline.

title: What makes a good question?
text:
Key points

Science is a process for reducing uncertainty, not a collection of facts
We test hypotheses by seeking disconfirmation, not confirmation
The biomass question — “Is it carbon-neutral?” — is genuinely open, and the answer depends on choices you’ll learn to identify

title: What do the numbers say?
section: What are we trying to do?
text:
What are we trying to do?
Compress thousands of numbers into a few useful ones.

Three questions about any dataset:

Where is the centre?
How spread out is it?
What shape is it?



[20 min block] This is bread-and-butter descriptive statistics. Keep it practical: every concept gets a geoscience example.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Centre: mean vs median


Mean
The “balance point.”
Sensitive to extremes.
Pull one value way up → mean shifts.


Median
The middle value.
Robust to extremes.
Pull one value way up → median barely moves.



When do they differ? When the distribution is skewed.


Example: UK household income. Mean is pulled up by high earners; median is more “typical.” Same with earthquake magnitudes — a few huge quakes pull the mean up.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Spread

Standard deviation — average distance from the mean
IQR — middle 50% of the data (robust to outliers)
Range — max minus min (sensitive to one extreme value)


Spread matters as much as centre. A mean of 10 with SD of 1 is very different from a mean of 10 with SD of 50.


Geoscience example: two boreholes both average 15°C, but one varies ±0.5°C and the other ±5°C. Very different stories.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Why spread matters


Figure 1

w02-spread.R



The means are identical, so a report quoting only the mean would describe these two boreholes with the same sentence.
Ask: which one would you drill next to? The answer is about spread, and there is no way to reach it from a table of means.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Shape


Figure 2

w02-distribution-shapes.R


Skewed: the mean chases the tail — income, grain size, ore grades.


Symmetric: mean ≈ median. Many natural processes.
Skewed: the long tail drags the mean away from the median. The median is the more “typical” value.
Bimodal: save this one — it sets up the next slide.
Key message: a mean without a histogram can be deeply misleading.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The two-humped problem


On the bimodal panel, the mean and median both land in the valley — a value that describes almost none of the data.

Two populations. Report one average and you have described neither.





Camelus bactrianus — PhyloPic, CC0





Always look at the distribution, not just the mean.



The camel is the mnemonic: a bactrian has two humps, and the point between them is not where the camel is.
Real geoscience example: a sediment sample with two source areas, or a borehole set spanning two formations. The grand mean is an artefact.
Ask: “What would you report instead?” Answer: identify the groups first, then summarise each. This previews Week 5 on confounders.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The More or Less principle



Tim Harford, who presents BBC Radio 4’s More or Less. PopTech, CC BY-SA 2.0

title: What do the numbers say?
section: A number without a comparator is meaningless.
text:
A number without a comparator is meaningless.


[15 min] This is the first key refrain. It should become a running question for the rest of the course.
Named after the BBC Radio 4 programme More or Less, which interrogates statistics in the news.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Try these
UK biomass electricity: 38 TWh/year.
Big or small? Compared to what?


Total UK electricity is ~320 TWh. So biomass ≈ 12%.



Present without context first. Let students guess. Then reveal the comparator.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Try these
Drax power station emits 12 Mt CO₂/year.


UK total CO₂: ~340 Mt. Drax is ~3.5% of the national total — from one building.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Try these
A single wind turbine produces about 6 GWh/year.


A UK household uses ~3,500 kWh/year. One turbine ≈ 1,700 homes.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The habit
Every time you see a number in this module, ask:

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
“Is that a big number?”
And its companion: “Compared to what?”

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
What makes a good figure?

Show the data — don’t just summarise
Make comparisons easy — same axes, same scales
Don’t distort — honest axes, honest encodings
Label clearly — axes, units, captions



[20 min block] Principles first, then live ggplot2 demo.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Bad figures



Truncated y-axes
Dual y-axes
3D bar charts
Pie charts for non-compositional data




Cherry-picked date ranges
Misleading area encodings
Missing labels or units
Colour that obscures rather than reveals




Four of these, right now. Three more in the exercise.


[6 min for the four pairs that follow] Two minutes each at most: show the bad chart, take one guess from the room, advance to the fixed version. The “Spot the lie” exercise later does the slower version with truncated axes, cherry-picked ranges and pie charts.
Each pair is the same numbers drawn twice. Say that out loud: no data was changed between the two slides.
Missing labels and units is the one rule with no pair here — it gets a before/after of its own in Week 4 and again in Week 10.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The dual axis


Figure 3

w02-dual-axis-bad.R



Ask: “Is the wood being burnt less efficiently every year?” That is what the chart appears to say.
Then ask what each axis starts at. The left starts at 0; the right starts at 6000 kt.
Nobody chose those two ranges together. That is the whole problem: a dual axis lets you pick the relationship you want to show.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The dual axis, fixed


Figure 4

w02-dual-axis-good.R


Fix: put both series on one scale. Indexed to 2015, imports and generation move together — which is what you would expect if the pellets are being burnt at a roughly constant efficiency.


TWh and kt cannot share an axis, so index them: divide by the first year and multiply by 100. Now both axes are “percent of 2015”.
The divergence in the first chart was manufactured entirely by the choice of axis ranges.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The 3D bar chart


Figure 5

w02-fake-3d-bad.R



Take a show of hands on gas versus wind before advancing. The room will say wind.
The perspective shrink is 10% per step back. The real gaps are 4% (gas over wind) and under 1% (nuclear over bioenergy), so the decoration is larger than the data.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The 3D bar chart, fixed


Figure 6

w02-fake-3d-good.R


Fix: no third dimension — there is no third variable. Where the gap is smaller than the ink, print the numbers.


Both rankings flip. A decorative choice reversed the answer to the question the chart was drawn to answer.
General rule: a third dimension is only honest if a third variable is being encoded. Depth for its own sake is noise added to a signal.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The area encoding


Figure 7

w02-area-encoding-bad.R



Ask for the impression first: roughly how much have imports grown? The room will say “doubled”, because the ink did.
The side is proportional to the value, so the area goes as the square: 1.42 across becomes 2.0 in area.
This is the standard infographic sin. It shows up with circles, tree icons and stacks of little power stations.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The area encoding, fixed


Figure 8

w02-area-encoding-good.R


Fix: encode with length from a common baseline. It is the one channel the eye reads accurately — and it comes with an axis to check.


If a pictogram is unavoidable, scale the area: side proportional to the square root of the value. Better still, don’t.
Note what the honest version gains beyond honesty: an axis, so a reader can extract a number rather than an impression.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Colour that obscures


Figure 9

w02-colour-obscures-bad.R



Ask: which origin stopped supplying the UK altogether? Give them ten seconds of squinting at the legend.
Rainbow hues are not ordered and not equally distinguishable. Red and green in the same chart also defeats the commonest colour vision deficiency — about 1 in 12 men.
Every series got a colour, so no series got emphasis.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Colour that reveals


Figure 10

w02-colour-obscures-good.R


Fix: colour the story, grey the context, label on the line. Colour is a scarce resource — spend it where the reader should look.


Same six series, nothing dropped. The grey lines still carry the context; they just stop competing.
Russia’s series ends after 2021, and the 2022 gap is filled from the USA and Latvia. That is visible here and invisible in the rainbow.
Direct labels beat a legend: no eye-travel, and no memory test.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Live demo: building a ggplot










Live code this. ggplot2 is already attached on this slide, and elec is loaded by the starter code. Build it step by step:

Start with geom_point() only
Add geom_line()
Add proper labels: labs(x = "Year", y = "Generation (TWh)")
Map colour to fuel type (requires reshaping — show briefly)

Keep to 3–4 builds. Narrate the “grammar”: data + aesthetics + geometries.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The grammar of graphics
ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ..., colour = ...)) +
  geom_point() +   # geometry
  labs(...)         # labels
Data + Aesthetics + Geometries = a plot.

Data: A plot is just one way of displaying the data. Analyses don’t start with “I’d like to see a bar chart”, but with “What do these data tell me?”


Aesthetics: Translation layer: Which variable controls which visual channel? Channels: x, y, colour, plotting symbol…
Establishes the rules – doesn’t plot anything itself.


Geometries: What physical mark displays the visual channels?


Everything in ggplot2 follows this pattern.


This is the mental model. Once they have this, they can build any plot by looking up the right geom_*().

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Instructions
I’ll show you some deliberately misleading charts.
For each one: what’s wrong, and how would you fix it?


[12 min] Quick-fire. Show each chart, give 60 seconds to think, then discuss — the next slide is always the fixed version, so hold it back until they have committed to an answer. This previews Week 4’s “how to lie with statistics” in a lighter form.
Could use a poll (Mentimeter/hands) for speed.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 1: The truncated axis


Figure 11

w02-truncated-axis.R



Let the chart sit for a moment. First reaction: “Generation is collapsing!” Then ask: what does the y-axis start at?
Don’t answer it here — advance to the fixed version.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 1, fixed


Figure 12

w02-truncated-axis-good.R


Fix: Start the y-axis at zero for bar charts. The bar’s length encodes the ratio, so a non-zero baseline breaks the encoding.


The y-axis in the previous slide began at 270 TWh. The actual drop from 2019 to 2024 is about 13% — noticeable, but not the catastrophe the chart implied.
Rule: bar lengths encode ratios. A non-zero baseline breaks that encoding. Line charts can sometimes justify a non-zero start, but bars never can.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 2: The cherry-picked date range


Figure 13

w02-cherry-picked-range.R



Three points, three years, a confident downward line. Ask what a reader would need to see to check it.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 2, fixed


Figure 14

w02-cherry-picked-range-good.R


Fix: Show the full time range. Bioenergy grew from 4 TWh (2000) to 40 TWh (2024) — a tenfold increase hidden by that window.


The dip is real: 2021–2023 genuinely falls. Cherry-picking does not require fake data, only a well-chosen window.
Shading the window rather than deleting it makes the point stick — the lie is visible inside the truth.
Ask: how would you decide, honestly, where a series should start? Best answer: at the start of the data, unless you can say why not.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 3: The misleading pie chart


Figure 15

w02-double-counted-pie.R



Ask: “How many slices include wind energy?” Answer: two (Wind and Low carbon). Same for nuclear, solar, and bioenergy.
The total shown is ~446 TWh; actual UK generation is 285 TWh.
General rule: pie chart slices must be mutually exclusive and sum to a meaningful 100%. If they don’t, use a bar chart.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Chart 3, fixed


Figure 16

w02-double-counted-pie-good.R


Fix: “Low carbon” double-counted Wind + Nuclear + Solar + Bioenergy, so the slices summed to 156%. An overlapping category is a shading, not a slice — and bars are sortable, labelable, and they add up.


“Other” is total generation minus the named fuels — computed, not asserted, so every TWh in the table is accounted for.
Note what the bar chart gains: you can read gas against wind directly, which is nearly impossible on a pie.
Pies are defensible for two or three parts of a genuine whole. Past that, bars.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Why distributions matter
A histogram shows you what the mean and SD cannot:

Is the data symmetric or skewed?
Are there outliers?
Is there more than one cluster?



[20 min block] Deeper dive into distributions. Connect to geoscience.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
The normal distribution
The familiar bell curve. Appears when many small, independent effects combine.

Central Limit Theorem (informally): averages of large samples tend toward normal, even if the underlying data aren’t.


This is why so many statistical tests assume normality — and why they often work even when the raw data are messy.


Don’t go deep into CLT. The intuition is enough: “averages smooth things out.”

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Log-normal distributions in geoscience
Many geological measurements are log-normal: skewed right, with a long tail of large values.

Grain size
Permeability
Ore grades
Earthquake magnitudes


When data are log-normal, the mean can be very different from the typical value.


The next slide is this claim as a picture: most of the rock in single figures of mD (millidarcy - unit of permeability), a tail into the thousands, and a mean well above almost every sample.
Connection to “Is that a big number?”: if the data are log-normal, the mean is a poor summary. The median or geometric mean is better.
Why ore grades are log-normal: geochemical enrichment works multiplicatively — each hydrothermal pulse or fractionation event multiplies the existing concentration by some factor. A chain of multiplications is equivalent to a sum of logs, and sums tend toward normal (CLT), so log(concentration) is normal → concentration is log-normal. Contrast with grain size and permeability, where it is energy averaging over many transport or flow events that produces the log-normal; the mechanism differs but the mathematics is the same.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
What that looks like


Figure 17

w02-log-normal.R



The mean is larger than 85% of the samples. It is not a typical permeability — it is not close to any of the rock. That is what “represents nobody” means.
The left panel is cut at the 99th percentile, and says so in the caption. Worth naming aloud: the honest way to crop a chart is to tell the reader you did.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
When to log-transform
If your data:

Are positive (no zeros or negatives)
Span several orders of magnitude
Are right-skewed


Then log() often makes them more symmetric and easier to analyse.


This comes back in Week 6 (t-test on log-transformed data) and Week 8 (regression diagnostics).

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Try it
Open WebR. Using the biomass data:

Make a histogram of one variable
Make a scatter plot of two variables with a colour mapping


This is a check that you’re comfortable with ggplot2 syntax before the application session.


[15 min] Hands-on. Circulate. Common issues: forgetting library("ggplot2"), wrong aesthetic mappings, confusion about fill vs colour.
Students who finish: try adding labels, changing the theme, or faceting by a categorical variable.

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Key points

Always look at the distribution, not just the mean
A number without a comparator is meaningless — “Is that a big number?”
ggplot2: data + aesthetics + geometries

title: What do the numbers say?
text:
Exit ticket
UK biomass electricity output was 37 TWh in 2024. A classmate says: “That’s a lot — it must be making a real difference.”
What’s the most important question to ask first?











PollEv.com/geol

37 TWh sounds large, but it is about 11% of UK electricity (~340 TWh/year in 2024). Significant, but not dominant.
Students who answer A are thinking about trends — not wrong, but it’s a secondary question. The comparator comes first.
This is the core “Is that a big number? Compared to what?” refrain in action. Use the result to reinforce it before sending them away.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
All measurements have uncertainty
The question is not whether there’s uncertainty — it’s how much and what kind.


[20 min block] Two types of error, then precision vs accuracy.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Two kinds of error


Systematic error (bias)
Your instrument is consistently wrong.
Example: emission factors that exclude the supply chain always underestimate true emissions.


Random error (noise)
Measurements vary each time.
Example: annual electricity generation fluctuates with weather, demand, and plant outages.




Systematic error is the sneaky one — you can’t detect it by repeating the measurement. You need an independent check.
Random error averages out with enough data. Systematic error doesn’t.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Precision vs accuracy


Precise but inaccurate
Measurements cluster tightly — but around the wrong value.
e.g., a miscalibrated thermometer


Accurate but imprecise
Measurements centre on the right value — but scatter widely.
e.g., noisy field readings




Always on target, or always into your own goal? Dominic Nelson, CC BY-SA 4.0




Which is worse? It depends on whether you can correct the bias.



Memorable example: Footballer hoofing in a long-range shot.

Precise, accurate: always on target
Equally precise, inaccurate: Always hoofs ball into own goal
Imprecise, accurate: Always gets it to right end of the pitch.
Imprecise, inaccurate [me]: Could end up anywhere

Geoscience examples: radiometric dating is precise but relies on assumptions about initial conditions (accuracy). Temperature records are accurate on average but have coverage gaps (precision).

title: How confident should we be?
text:
All four combinations


Figure 1

w03-precision-accuracy.R



Point at the precise-but-inaccurate panel: repeating the measurement makes it look better and does nothing to the error. That is the whole danger of systematic bias in one picture.
The dashed line is a real formation mean from borehole_temp.csv, not a round number chosen to look tidy.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The biomass emission factor


Figure 2

w03-emission-factors.R


“What are the sources of uncertainty in this number?”

Work in pairs. 5 minutes. Then share.


The number in question is biomass’s zero. If you get stuck, thinking about how the other numbers are calculated might help you to think of aspects you’ve overlooked.
[15 min] Expected answers: what’s included in lifecycle emissions? Transport? Land use change? Drying? Regrowth? Different studies give different numbers — why?
Classify each as systematic or random.
This is the pivot point: students start to realise the “zero” emission factor is a policy choice, not a measurement.
UNFCCC = United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change DESNZ = UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The courtroom analogy


In a trial

Start with “innocent”
Look at the evidence
Decide: enough to convict?



In statistics

Start with “no effect” (null hypothesis)
Look at the data
Decide: enough to reject the null?






The Jury (1861), John Morgan — Buckinghamshire County Museum, public domain




[20 min block] This is conceptual — no formulae yet. The goal is to build intuition for why we need formal testing.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Two types of mistake









Null is true
Null is false




Reject null
✘ Type I error(false positive)
✔ Correct


Don’t reject
✔ Correct
✘ Type II error(false negative)






Type I: Convicting an innocent person.
Claiming one ridgetop site is windier than the next when they’re the same.


Type II: Acquitting a guilty one.
Missing a real difference because your sample was too small.




Type I: Null = innocence; rejection = convict
Type II: Null = innocence; acceptance = release
The significance level (α, usually 0.05) is our threshold for Type I error — how much surprise we require.
Type II error depends on sample size, effect size, and variability. We’ll formalise this later; for now, the intuition is enough.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
What does “overlap” look like?


Figure 3

w03-overlap.R


At-chimney emissions: CO₂ measured as it leaves the plant. Same means in each panel (Coal: 910; Biomass: 1000 kg CO₂/MWh).


The question: is this difference bigger than we’d expect by chance?


What the figure shows. Both centres are at-chimney emission factors read from emission_factors.csv: biomass combustion_only and coal official, which DESNZ defines as combustion only. That is what a stack monitor would read at the point of combustion — the CO₂ physically leaving the plant per MWh generated.
It is deliberately not lifecycle or net accounting. No supply chain, no regrowth credit, no UNFCCC zero. Say the term out loud — “at-chimney emissions” — because the rest of the module turns on the difference between this and the net figures we meet next session.
Expect the “that looks wrong” reaction. Biomass is higher than coal at the chimney, and that is correct: wood holds less energy per unit of carbon than coal, so a MWh from pellets sends modestly more CO₂ up the stack. Nothing about the chimney makes biomass cleaner — the entire case for biomass rests on the regrowth argument, which is exactly why it deserves scrutiny. (materials/carbon-accounting-summary.md has the derivation if someone asks.)
Only the spread is invented. The question is what a fixed difference looks like at two levels of variability.
“Would you bet these are different?” Ask it of each panel in turn. The gap between the centres is identical — only the spread changes.
The shaded band is where a single measurement tells you nothing: it could have come from either kind of plant. Verbal example: it’s not unlikely that I’d get a measurement of X from biomass and Y from coal, reversing the true order of the means.
Just visual intuition for now: we’ll formalize this mathematically in Week 6.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The scenario
You measure at-chimney emissions from 5 biomass plants and 5 coal plants.
The biomass mean is higher. But there’s overlap.


Are you convinced?



[10 min] Let students discuss in small groups, then collect responses.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
What if…

What if you measured 50 of each?
What if the difference were twice as large?
What if one measurement were an extreme outlier?



Couch this in “precision vs. accuracy” - what would we gain here?
Ability to discriminate; confounders?



Sample size, effect size, and variability all matter.
We’ll formalise this in Week 6 — for now, trust your intuition that eyeballing isn’t good enough.


The point: students should leave feeling “I can see why we need formal tests” — which motivates Week 6’s t-tests.
Don’t resolve the disagreement neatly. The tension is productive.

title: How confident should we be?
section: Where did your data come from?
text:
Where did your data come from?
And does it represent what you think it represents?


[20 min block] Population vs sample, selection bias, survivorship bias, confounding.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Population vs sample


You have data from Drax — one power station.

Can you generalise to “biomass electricity”?



Drax produces ~86% of UK biomass electricity. Does that help or hurt?






One power station, standing in for a whole fuel. © Drax





It helps (the sample is most of the population) but it also means Drax is unusual — it’s massive, purpose-built, and uses a specific supply chain. Other biomass plants may behave very differently.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Selection bias


If you only measure the biggest, best-known facility, your results may not generalise.

Survivorship bias: if failing biomass plants shut down and disappear from the data, the remaining ones look better than average.


Confounding: biomass plants might be newer than coal plants. Any efficiency difference might reflect age, not fuel.






Every boat in the harbour survived the storm. Royal Navy / MOD, OGL v1.0





Older, or worse built? The fuel is not the only thing that differs. AI-generated (Gemini/Nano Banana 2)






Geological parallel: sampling only exposed rock faces — weathered, accessible, atypical of the subsurface.
These are the same issues HolmesCo will demonstrate in Week 5 (valley boreholes, convenience sampling).

title: How confident should we be?
text:
The carbon accounting rule
The standard framework: CO₂ from burning biomass is counted as zero at the point of combustion.

Work in pairs:

List the assumptions this framework makes
For each: is it testable? What evidence would challenge it?
Which assumptions, if wrong, would most change the conclusion?



[15 min] This directly feeds Week 3 app (scenario analysis) and Week 4 (the briefing).
Expected assumptions: trees regrow (timescale?), supply chain emissions are negligible, land use doesn’t change, the alternative fuel would have been burned anyway.
The “if wrong, most changes the conclusion” question is the key one. It teaches students to prioritise assumptions by impact.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
What did you find?





Type 3–4 assumptions in as students call them out. Students will need them for the application session (scenario analysis) and the Week 4 briefing.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
“What assumptions are we making?”
This is the question that separates good analysis from bad.

title: How confident should we be?
text:
Key points

All measurements have uncertainty — the question is how much
Systematic error is more dangerous than random error
The biomass “zero” is an assumption, not a measurement
Next step: what happens when we change the assumptions?

title: How confident should we be?

Exit ticket
A lifecycle assessment reports that UK biomass electricity produces 0 gCO₂/kWh. What is the most important thing to check before accepting this number?











PollEv.com/geol

The “zero” is not a measurement — it is a policy assumption that depends entirely on what is included (combustion only? transport? processing? regrowth?) and over what time horizon.
D (peer review) is a reasonable instinct but wrong as the most important thing — a peer-reviewed paper can still use a narrow system boundary.
This question directly tests whether students have internalised “What assumptions are we making?” as a reflexive question.

title: Making the case
text:
Who is your reader?
A policy-maker: busy, not a specialist, needs to make a decision.

What they need:

A clear bottom line
Evidence they can trust
Honest acknowledgement of uncertainty



[20 min block] Writing for non-specialists. This is the communication strand coming to a head.

title: Making the case
text:
Structure of a policy briefing



Section
Purpose




Summary
The answer — first. Reader could stop here.


Evidence
Figures, data, analysis


Caveats
What’s uncertain, what depends on assumptions


Conclusions
Recommendation, with caveats attached




Compare to an academic paper: background first, answer last.
A briefing is the opposite — answer first, evidence after.


Key principle: “Your reader should be able to stop after the summary and still know the main message.”
The next slide is a real briefing in exactly this shape. Open it live — preview-links: auto means the link opens in-frame.

title: Making the case
text:
A real parliamentary briefing
Governance of solar radiation modification research — POSTnote 773, Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology, 13 July 2026.
https://post.parliament.uk/research-briefings/post-pn-0773/ · DOI 10.58248/PN773




POST’s sections
Our structure




Overview and key points
Summary — the answer, first


How the research is conducted; funding figures
Evidence


Geopolitics; ethics and legislation
Caveats


What has been tried already
Conclusions





The point of this slide is that the four-part shape (summary → evidence → caveats → conclusions) is general.
POSTnotes are peer reviewed and list their contributors at the end of the briefing. That is what “evidence they can trust” looks like in practice.

title: Making the case
text:
The summary test

If your reader stops after the first paragraph, do they know:

What you investigated?
What you found?
What you recommend?




This is the standard for a good summary. If any of the three are missing, the summary needs work.
Keep the three questions live for the rest of the session. The two exemplar reports are built so that this test separates them: the faithful summary answers all three, the traitor’s answers only the middle one — loudly. Students who apply the test catch it; students who read for tone do not.

title: Making the case
text:
10 minutes
Write a 3–4 sentence summary of your biomass findings, aimed at a government minister.

Then we’ll share a few.

Is the message clear? Is the uncertainty honest? Would a minister know what to do?



[15 min including sharing] Students write, then 2–3 volunteers share. Class gives quick feedback using the three questions above.

title: Making the case
text:
Same data – two conclusions
Two reports present the same data in different ways.
Both are technically accurate.
One is honest. The other is not.


In pairs or threes, annotate: - What does each report do well? - Where is it dishonest?

Links: Pro-AI | Anti-AI


[25 min block] This is the exemplar reveal. Use the faithful and traitor AI environmental impact reports.
Take your time. Let students react. The moment they realise the traitor report “feels” more convincing is pedagogically powerful.

title: Making the case
text:
Two exemplar reports


Faithful report
Balanced evidence. Honest caveats. Uncertain where the data are uncertain.


Traitor report
Selective evidence. Misleading framing. Confident where it shouldn’t be.




Ardross Castle, where The Traitors is filmed. Derek Spence / Geograph, CC BY-SA 2.0




Let’s look at the techniques.


Show both reports (or excerpts) side by side. Students read briefly, then you walk through the techniques.

title: Making the case
text:
Technique 1: Cherry-picking
Choose the number that tells your story.

Example: AI energy per query — 0.3 Wh (a Google search) vs 18.9 Wh (a complex AI task). Same topic, 60× difference, depending on which you cite.


The traitor report cited the smaller number to downplay AI’s energy cost. The faithful report cited the range.

title: Making the case
text:
Technique 2: Invalid chart type


A pie chart of things that don’t form a whole.








Figure 1






w02-double-counted-pie.R



Or a bar chart where the y-axis doesn’t start at zero.








Figure 2






w02-truncated-axis.R




The chart is “technically correct” but visually lies.


Both of these are the Week 2 “spot the lie” charts, unchanged. Say so: the point of a callback is that they diagnosed these themselves two weeks ago and are now being asked to imagine drawing one on purpose.

title: Making the case
text:
Technique 3: Cross-scale conflation
Compare a small thing to a big thing without adjusting the scale.

Example: “Global AI uses less electricity than UK households.”
Both are true numbers — but the comparison is meaningless without matching the scales (global vs national).

title: Making the case
text:
Technique 4: Omission
What you don’t show matters as much as what you do.

Example: Omit the supply chain, the payback period, or the alternative scenario. The remaining evidence looks cleaner — and more convincing.


Don’t reveal all the techniques in the teaching notes — save some for the application session reveal, when students have had a chance to spot them during peer review.

title: Making the case
text:
The lesson

The most dangerous misinformation is technically sourced.
You can’t just fact-check the numbers — you have to audit the choices.



This connects everything: Week 1 (falsifiability), Week 2 (“Compared to what?”), Week 3 (“What assumptions?”).
The skills for spotting deception are the same skills for avoiding it accidentally.

title: Making the case
text:
Spot the omission


Figure 3

w03-emission-factors.R


What’s been left out? How does the omission change the impression?



[10 min] Small-group discussion. Every number on this chart is correct and sourced. What is missing is the supply chain and the payback period — the two columns of emission_factors.csv this view does not touch.
The sting: this is their own Week 2 chart, and they met the fuller picture in Week 3. The omission they are diagnosing is one they made.

title: Making the case
text:
Principles (revisited)

Every figure needs a “so what” — what should the reader take from it?
Don’t show everything. Show the thing that matters.
Captions tell the story, not just the axes.
Label directly rather than relying on legends.

text:
Before and after





Before


After














Figure 6















Figure 7










Same data, same file. What changed — and which change did the most work?










Series
All six fuels
The four largest by mean over 2000–2024


Legend order
Alphabetical by column name — nothing to do with size
Largest mean first


Y axis
twh
Generation (TWh)


Words
None
A subtitle saying what to look at; a named source


Panel
Default grey
White, faint gridlines






w04-figure-before.R · w04-figure-after.R



Spend the time on the first row. Ranking the fuels by their mean over the whole period rather than by 2024 is not a cosmetic choice. Rank on 2024 and coal drops out — 2.0 TWh, sixth place — and the headline becomes “wind has nearly caught gas”, a 3 TWh gap.
Rank on the mean and coal is back in second place, and you can see the thing that actually happened: coal and wind swapped, around 2015. Wind now out-generates coal roughly forty times over.
So: the honest chart is the one that picked its four fuels by a rule chosen before looking at which story it produced. Both rules are defensible. Only one of them was written down first.
This is the Week 2 refrain arriving in their own work: compared to what? And the Week 4 refrain: audit the choices, not just the numbers.
Also note the importance of colour: this uses the Durham palette. My first draft swapped the colours of coal and gas - semantic linkage made this hard to read!

title: Making the case
text:
Your assignment
Write a ~2-page policy briefing answering:
“Is UK biomass electricity carbon-neutral?”

title: Making the case
text:
Peer review
You will each be assigned two classmates’ briefings.
One Issue per briefing — clarity, evidence, uncertainty, verdict.

The Issue starts with three lines a script reads:
Reviewer: your-username
Verdict: FAITHFUL          (or SUSPECT)
Argues: CARBON-NEUTRAL     (or NOT-CARBON-NEUTRAL / MIXED)


Labour the three header lines. They are how the reveal gets built, and a mangled line drops that review out of the class data.
Verdict and Argues are separate on purpose — flag that now, come back to it in the reveal.

title: Making the case
text:
Two questions, not one

Do you believe it? — and, separately — what is it arguing?


A briefing can reach the conclusion you already hold and still be a traitor’s.


This is the whole reason Argues exists as a field. Students reliably conflate “I agree with the conclusion” with “this is honest”, and the reveal chart is built to show them doing it.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The logic of comparison
You can’t know if something is big unless you measure something else.


[20 min block] Experimental design fundamentals.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Controls
What you hold constant so you can isolate the variable of interest.

Example: comparing wind farm output across sites.



Control for
Why




Turbine model
Different models have different capacities


Terrain
Ridgetop vs valley affects wind speed


Grid curtailment
Some farms are told to stop generating





What can’t you control? Weather. Maintenance schedules.


Geoscience angle: in field sciences we rarely get true experiments. We observe natural variation and try to isolate factors. This makes design more important, not less.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Treatment vs control groups


Lab sciences
Treatment group gets the intervention.
Control group doesn’t.
Random assignment.


Field sciences
“Treatment” is often a natural condition.
“Control” is a comparison group.
You can’t randomise geology.




Because we can’t randomise, we need to think harder about what might confound our comparisons. That’s next.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The scenario


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Ground Investigation Report — Proposed Wind Farm, County Durham
HolmesCo drilled 3 boreholes in the valley where access roads already exist. All three encountered competent sandstone.
Conclusion: “Bedrock across the site is suitable for turbine foundations.”



What’s wrong with this? Work in pairs — 5 minutes.



[15 min] Expected problems: (a) boreholes are in the valley, turbines are on ridgetops; (b) 3 is tiny; (c) convenience sampling;

no control site. What would a better investigation look like?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The problems

Selection bias: sampled where it was convenient, not representative
Wrong location: boreholes in the valley, turbines on the ridgetops
Tiny sample: 3 boreholes for a multi-km² site
No comparison: how do we know this is unusually good (or bad)?

title: Designing your investigation
text:
What is a confounder?
A variable that is correlated with both the treatment and the outcome.
You can’t tell which caused the effect.


[20 min block] Confounders are the hidden trap in observational studies.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Classic examples








Observation
Apparent cause
Real cause (confounder)




Ice cream sales ↑, drowning ↑
Ice cream causes drowning?
Hot weather


More solar panels → higher GDP
Solar causes wealth?
Latitude, governance, investment


Deeper boreholes → higher temp
Depth causes heat?
Location (geothermal area)




Correlation is not causation — because of confounders.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The borehole case, both ways


Figure 1

w05-confounder.R



Same points in both panels. Nothing was added or removed — only the question changed, from “how does temperature vary with depth?” to “how does it vary with depth within a region?”
Both trends are fitted by lm(). The flat lines are a result, not a drawing.
This is the slide that earns the next one: stratification is the right-hand panel.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
How to handle confounders

Randomisation — when possible (rare in geoscience)
Stratification — compare within subgroups
Matching — pair similar observations
Acknowledgement — when all else fails, be honest about what you can’t control



Option 4 is the most common in geoscience and policy analysis. Honesty about confounders is itself a research skill.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Three scenarios
For each: identify the confounder and suggest how to address it.

1. “Communities near wind farms report more headaches than communities without wind farms.”


Confounders: rural/urban, age, awareness/nocebo effect, reporting bias.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Scenario 2
2. “Countries with higher nuclear capacity have lower carbon emissions per capita.”

Confounders: GDP, industrialisation stage, energy mix decisions driven by geography and politics.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
Scenario 3
3. “Students who use AI assistants score higher on coding assignments.”

Confounders: prior coding experience, motivation, time spent on assignments.


[15 min total] Quick discussion for each. Don’t linger — the point is pattern recognition, not exhaustive analysis.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
How to choose your sample








Strategy
How
When




Random
Every unit has equal probability
Gold standard; often impractical


Stratified
Sample within each subgroup
Ensures representation


Systematic
Every nth unit
Regular grids, monitoring stations


Convenience
Whatever’s easiest
HolmesCo’s default





[20 min block] Practical sampling. The key message: your sampling strategy is a decision you must justify.

title: Designing your investigation
text:
The same site, four ways


Figure 2

w05-sampling-strategies.R



Random and systematic are the pair the table cannot separate: both are “unbiased”, and they look nothing alike. Note the gaps in the random panel — that is what stratification exists to prevent.
The convenience panel is the next slide. Ask what question that sample can answer, and about what area.

The HolmesCo default
“We sampled these because they were there.”

Honest — but weak.



Your sampling strategy is a decision you must justify in your report.



This connects directly to Phase 2: students will need to explain why they chose their data sources and whether their sample is representative.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
What does a t-test do?
Compares two group means and asks:

“Is this difference larger than we’d expect by chance?”



[25 min block] The t-test, step by step, with a live demo.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
The logic

Assume no difference (null hypothesis)
Calculate how far apart the means are, relative to the variability (→ t-statistic)
Ask: if there were really no difference, how often would we see a t this extreme? (→ p-value)

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Live demo










Type this, don’t paste it. Say out loud that the students have the same dataset open; invite them to get to the p-value first, and start typing a minute in.
Anticipated code:
borehole <- read.csv("data/borehole_temp.csv")

ggplot(borehole, aes(x = formation, y = temperature_c)) +
  geom_boxplot()

t.test(temperature_c ~ formation, data = borehole)
ggplot2 is already attached on this slide, and the boxplot call is the one exercises/week6-app.qmd Exercise 1 asks for.
Show the output: t-statistic, df, p-value, confidence interval.
Interpret aloud: “The mean difference is 8.4°C, with a 95% CI of [0.9, 16.0]. The p-value is 0.03, meaning we’d see a difference this large about 3% of the time if there were truly no difference.”
Exact values, so the next slide’s table matches: t = 2.2419, df = 47.179, p = 0.0297, CI [0.865, 15.969], means 35.30 (Stainmore) and 26.88 (Whin Sill).

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Reading the output
t = 2.24, df = 47.2, p-value = 0.030
95% CI: [0.86, 15.97]




Element
Meaning




t-statistic
How many SEs apart are the means


p-value
How surprising, if H₀ is true


95% CI
Plausible range for the true difference





Emphasise: the CI is often more useful than the p-value. It tells you the size of the effect, not just whether it exists.
These are the real numbers from borehole_temp.csv, so they should match the live demo exactly. If they don’t, the data changed.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
What “how often” means


Figure 1

w06-t-distribution.R



Step 3 of “The logic” was: if there were really no difference, how often would we see a t this extreme? That “how often” is an area, and this is it.
Both tails, because the question was “this extreme”, not “this large”.
t, df and the shaded fraction all come from the same t.test() the demo just ran.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Write one sentence
I’m showing you R output from a t-test.
Write one sentence interpreting this result for a policy audience.

Then we’ll compare.


[10 min] Show pre-prepared output on screen. Students write, then share.
Common mistake to watch for: “the p-value means there’s a 3% chance the null is true.” Flag this — it’s exactly the confusion block 3 will address.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
A common mistake

“p = 0.03 means there’s a 3% chance the null is true.”


Wrong. But extremely common. We’ll come back to this.


Plant the seed now. The base rate fallacy in block 3 will explain why this interpretation is wrong.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Every test rests on assumptions
For the t-test:

Independence — observations don’t influence each other
Normality — data within each group are roughly normal
Equal variance — groups have similar spread (Student’s t; Welch’s t relaxes this)



[20 min block] Assumptions, how to check, what to do when violated.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
How to check



Assumption
Check




Normality
Histogram, QQ plot, shapiro.test()


Equal variance
Side-by-side boxplots, Levene’s test


Independence
Think about the study design

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
When assumptions are violated
A skewed variable can produce misleading p-values.


Figure 2

w06-skew-and-logs.R



This is the dataset from the live demo. The test they just ran is the one that breaks: p = 0.030 raw, p = 0.22 logged. Both p-values are computed by the script.
Nothing was removed and no outlier was excluded. The only change is the scale the test was run on.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
HolmesCo made the same mistake


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Statistical Analysis — Soil Permeability
t-test on raw values: p = 0.04 → “Significant difference!”
t-test on log-transformed values: p = 0.23 → “No significant difference.”
The “significant” result was an artefact of skewness.



This is a vivid example. HolmesCo tested permeability (always log-normal) without transforming. The p-value changed from 0.04 to 0.23 — the “discovery” vanished.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
In WebR
Given a dataset:

Make histograms of each group
Decide whether to transform
Run t.test() before and after transformation
Compare: did the conclusion change?



[10 min] Quick hands-on exercise. The WebR page has the scaffolded version with hints.

title: Testing hypotheses
section: The most important 25 minutes of the course
text:
The most important 25 minutes of the course
I’m going to show you why a statistically significant result can still be wrong most of the time.


[25 min block] Take your time. This is the intellectual centrepiece of the module. Let the numbers sink in.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Warm-up: Monty Hall
Some of you simulated the Monty Hall problem in first-year Python.

Switching wins 2/3 of the time. But your gut says 50/50.


Why? Because your gut ignores the information the host gave you when they opened a door.


That confusion — between P(win) and P(win | what you now know) — is exactly what this block is about.


Brief connection. Don’t re-derive Monty Hall. The point: conditional probability is unintuitive, and this has serious consequences.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
The medical test
A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people.
A test is 99% accurate (99% sensitivity, 99% specificity).
You test positive.


What’s the probability you have the disease?

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Cast your vote











PollEv.com/geol
text geol to 07480 781235





Activate the poll before showing this slide. Use a numeric open-ended response so answers appear as a histogram.
Most students will cluster around 95–99%. A few may guess lower. The spread makes the reveal (“it’s 9%”) land much harder — they can see on screen that almost everyone got it wrong.
Wait until responses plateau, then advance to the arithmetic.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
The arithmetic
Out of 100,000 people:




Has disease
No disease
Total




Test positive
99
999
1,098


Test negative
1
98,901
98,902


Total
100
99,900
100,000




P(disease | positive) = 99 / 1,098 ≈ 9%


Not 99%. Nine percent.


Let this land. Pause. “Why is it so low?”

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Why is it so low?
Because the disease is rare.
The base rate matters enormously.


Figure 3

w06-base-rate.R


Even a very accurate test produces many false positives when the condition is uncommon.


The 9% from the previous slide is the marked point. Same test, same 99% accuracy, everywhere on this curve — only the population changes.
Ask where they would have to move along the axis to get the 99% they guessed in the poll. It is a condition affecting most of the room.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
HolmesCo strikes gold


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Press Release — Major Gold Discovery in County Durham!
“Our geochemical assay (95% accuracy) detected gold in 50 out of 10,000 soil samples. Confirmed multi-element anomaly!”



Work through the numbers on the board or next slide.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
The reality
Suppose 5 in 10,000 samples are actually gold-bearing.





Gold present
No gold
Total




Assay positive
~5
~500
~505


Assay negative
~0
~9,495
~9,495





HolmesCo’s 50 positives? Almost certainly all false.


The press release is nonsense.


The 50 “hits” is actually fewer than the ~500 expected false positives. If anything, the assay is underperforming.
This is the Week 6 equivalent of the traitor reveal.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Connection to p-values
A p-value tells you: P(data | H₀)
How surprising is this data if the null is true?

What you actually want: P(H₀ | data)
How likely is the null to be true given this data?



These are not the same thing. The difference depends on the base rate.



Key sentence: “If you’re testing an implausible hypothesis, a significant p-value is probably a false positive. If you’re testing something well-supported, a significant result is more convincing.”

title: Testing hypotheses
text: The new refrain

title: Testing hypotheses
section: “How plausible was this before we tested?”
text:
“How plausible was this before we tested?”


This is the Bayesian insight without the formula. The habit of asking about prior plausibility is what matters.
This also sets up Week 7: if you run 20 tests, the base rate for any individual hypothesis being true is low → false positives accumulate.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
For your project
Discuss with your group:

What comparison will you test?
What’s your null hypothesis?
What’s your prior expectation — plausible or a long shot?
What assumptions should you check?

Write 3–4 sentences.


[10 min] This feeds directly into the application session.

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Key points

A t-test compares two groups — but check the assumptions first
A p-value is P(data | H₀), not P(H₀ | data)
The base rate determines whether a “significant” result is real
Always ask: “How plausible was this before I tested?”

title: Testing hypotheses
text:
Exit ticket
A t-test comparing two groups returns p = 0.04. Which statement is correct?











PollEv.com/geol
text geol to 07480 781235





Correct answer: B — P(data | H₀), not P(H₀ | data).
A is the classic confusion of P(data | H₀) with P(H₀ | data). Very common, even among experienced researchers.
C conflates statistical significance with practical or scientific significance — and ignores the base rate argument from this session.
D inverts the conditional probability (like A, but from the other direction).
If many students answer A or D, revisit the medical test example: “If the disease has a 1-in-1000 base rate, a positive test is probably still a false positive — even though p < 0.05.”

title: Comparing groups
text:
The problem
Three groups (e.g., wind farms in three regions).
You could run three pairwise t-tests: A vs B, A vs C, B vs C.

Each test has a 5% false positive rate.


Three tests: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − 0.95³ ≈ 14%
Ten tests: 40%
Twenty tests: 64%


[20 min block] Multiple comparisons. Build to the HolmesCo mineral survey.

title: Comparing groups
text:
The escalation



Number of tests
P(≥1 false positive)




1
5%


3
14%


10
40%


20
64%


100
99.4%




Run enough tests and you’re guaranteed to “find” something.

title: Comparing groups
text:
HolmesCo’s mineral survey


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Press Release — Multi-Element Anomaly Discovered!
“We tested soil samples from 20 sites for enrichment in 20 elements. We found statistically significant enrichment (p < 0.05) for three elements at one site!”



If there’s truly nothing there, how many significant results would you expect by chance?



20 elements × 20 sites = 400 tests × 0.05 = 20 expected false positives. Three hits is fewer than expected by chance. HolmesCo’s “discovery” actually underperforms random noise.

title: Comparing groups
text:
The answer
20 × 20 = 400 tests at α = 0.05
Expected false positives: 20
HolmesCo found 3.

That’s fewer than expected by chance. The “discovery” is noise.


Let this land. The subversion — that the result is actually less than chance — makes the multiple comparisons problem viscerally clear.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Your project

How many comparisons are you planning to make?


If you run all of them at α = 0.05, what’s your family-wise false positive rate?


Formula: 1 − (1 − α)k where k = number of tests


[10 min] Students calculate for their own projects. Then discuss: “If you’re testing more than one thing, you need to account for it.”

title: Comparing groups
text:
One test for multiple groups
ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) asks:

“Does any group differ from the others?”

Without specifying which.


[20 min block] ANOVA mechanics, live demo, post-hoc tests.

title: Comparing groups
text:
The logic

Total variation = between groups + within groups
If between-group variation is large relative to within-group → at least one group is different
The F-statistic captures this ratio
The p-value tells you how surprising this F is under the null

title: Comparing groups
text:
“Relative to within”


Figure 1

w07-f-ratio.R



Check the mean bars against each other across the panels: same height. The between-group part of the ratio is held fixed by construction — the script scales one set of residuals rather than drawing twice.
Both F values come from aov() on the panel’s own points.
Ask which panel you would be willing to call a real regional difference, before showing any p-value.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Live demo








If significant → which pairs differ?


Type this live, don’t paste it. Students have wind_output.csv on their own exercise page — tell them to race you to the F value.
Anticipated code:
wind <- read.csv("data/wind_output.csv")

model <- aov(capacity_pct ~ region, data = wind)
summary(model)

TukeyHSD(model)
The slide previously showed aov(output ~ region, data = wind_df) — neither the object nor the column exists. The real data is wind$capacity_pct by wind$region, matching exercises/week7-content.qmd.
Numbers: F(3, 96) = 14.21, p = 9.76e-08. Tukey’s adjusted p-values give two clusters — Scotland vs Northern England is the only non-significant pair (p = 0.994) and Wales vs Southern England the only other one above 0.05 (p = 0.673); the four north-vs-south comparisons are all significant.
Read the pairwise comparisons out loud. Point out the adjusted p-values: that adjustment is the whole reason we are not running six separate t-tests.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Corrections for multiple comparisons








Method
How
When




Tukey’s HSD
All pairwise, designed for ANOVA
After a significant ANOVA


Bonferroni
Divide α by number of tests
Simple, conservative, any context




Both reduce the false positive rate by being stricter about what counts as significant.


Don’t go deep into the math. The key idea: when you test multiple things, you raise the bar for each individual test.

title: Comparing groups
text:
In WebR
Provided dataset: wind farm output in four regions.

Visualise with boxplots
Run aov()
Is it significant?
Run TukeyHSD() — which pairs differ?
Write a one-sentence conclusion



[15 min] Hands-on. The WebR exercise page has scaffolding.

title: Comparing groups
text: “Significant” ≠ “important”

title: Comparing groups
section: A p-value tells you whether an effect is detectable.
text: A p-value tells you whether an effect is detectable.

title: Comparing groups
section: It does not tell you whether it’s big enough to matter.
text:
It does not tell you whether it’s big enough to matter.


[20 min block] Effect sizes — the statistical formalisation of “Is that a big number?”

title: Comparing groups
text:
The HolmesCo temperature problem


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Two boreholes, 1,000 readings each.
Mean difference: 0.02°C. p-value: 0.001.
“Highly significant temperature anomaly detected!”


Is 0.02°C meaningful for any practical purpose?


With enough data, trivially small differences become “significant.” The p-value says “detectable,” not “important.”

title: Comparing groups
text:
Cohen’s d
A standardised measure of how far apart two groups are:



d
Interpretation




0.2
Small


0.5
Medium


0.8
Large




effectsize::cohens_d(y ~ group, data = df)


d = (mean₁ − mean₂) / pooled SD. It answers “how many standard deviations apart are the groups?”

title: Comparing groups
text:
What those numbers look like


Figure 2

w07-cohens-d.R



The point is the right-hand panel. “Large” still leaves two groups overlapping across most of their range — so a significant result with d = 0.8 does not mean you can tell an individual’s group from their measurement.
The shared percentage is integrated from the curves, not asserted.

title: Comparing groups
text:
For ANOVA: η² (eta-squared)
Proportion of variance explained by the grouping variable.



η²
Interpretation




0.01
Small


0.06
Medium


0.14
Large





Always report both the p-value and an effect size.
A policy-maker needs to know “how big?” — not just “is it real?”



Link to “Is that a big number?” from Week 2. Same habit, formalised.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Three test results


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Technical Summary

Test A: p = 0.002, Cohen’s d = 1.2
Test B: p = 0.04, Cohen’s d = 0.08
Test C: p = 0.08, 95% CI = [−0.3, 6.1]



For each: should we act on this? Why or why not?


[15 min] A is significant with a large effect — act. B is significant but trivially small — maybe not. C is non-significant but the CI almost excludes zero — worth investigating further.

title: Comparing groups
text:
Key points

Multiple tests inflate false positives — correct for them
ANOVA compares multiple groups in one test; TukeyHSD finds which differ
Significance ≠ importance — always report effect sizes
“Is that a big number?” now has a formal answer

This week: models.
A model is a simplified story about how the world works. The question is always: how much does it capture, and what does it leave out?


[5 min] Frame the session: models as simplifications. Every equation in science is a model. Every test contains an implicit model.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What is a model?
A deliberate simplification that captures some features of reality and ignores others.

Every statistical test you’ve run contains an implicit model.
The t-test models data as two normal distributions with equal variance.
Now we make the model explicit.


[20 min block] Linear regression — concept and live demo.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Linear regression
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\]

“y increases by β₁ for every one-unit increase in x, plus noise.”


That’s the whole model. It’s powerful — and limited.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Live demo










Type this, don’t paste it. The students have elec on their own page; tell them to beat you to the R² and start typing a minute in.
Anticipated code:
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")

ggplot(elec, aes(x = year, y = bioenergy_twh)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

model <- lm(bioenergy_twh ~ year, data = elec)
summary(model)
The slide previously showed lm(output ~ windspeed, data = turbine_df) and claimed R² ≈ 0.6. No such dataset exists in this repo, so no one could ever have run it. Biomass over time is real data the students already know from Week 1.
Numbers: slope 1.713 TWh per year, R² = 0.921, p = 3.6e-14, residual SE 3.77 on 23 df. “Biomass generation has risen about 1.7 TWh a year, and a straight line accounts for 92% of the variation.”
Deliberately not the solar data — that is Exercise 1 in a few slides’ time, and its negative slope should surprise them.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Reading the output



Element
Meaning




Intercept (β₀)
Predicted y when x = 0


Slope (β₁)
Change in y per unit change in x


R²
Proportion of variance explained


p-value (slope)
Is the slope distinguishable from zero?





Emphasise R² interpretation: “R² = 0.6 means 60% of the variation is explained. 40% is something else.”

title: Models and their limits
text:
Solar panels and temperature
Solar panel output vs temperature — counterintuitive.

Make a scatter plot
Fit lm()
Interpret the slope and R²
Plot the fit



Is the relationship linear? Does the model capture the pattern?



[15 min] Output decreases at high temperatures for crystalline silicon panels. Students discover a negative slope where they expected positive. Good moment to ask “Did the data surprise you?”

title: Models and their limits
text:
The four assumptions

Linearity — the relationship is actually linear
Independence — residuals don’t influence each other
Homoscedasticity — constant variance of residuals
Normality of residuals (for inference)



[20 min block] Assumptions, diagnostic plots, what to do when violated.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Diagnostic plots








Four plots, two that matter most:







Plot
What to look for




Residuals vs Fitted
Pattern = non-linearity or heteroscedasticity


QQ plot
Departures from the line = non-normal residuals





Anticipated code — one line, and model is still in the session from the live demo a few slides back:
plot(model)
If the session has been reset, re-run the demo cell first.
Walk through each plot. “No pattern in residuals vs fitted = good. Points on the QQ line = good.”
Biomass over time is a useful case here: R² is 0.92 and the residuals-vs-fitted panel still curves, because growth was flat then steep. High R², wrong shape — which is the point of the whole session.

title: Models and their limits
text:
The scenario


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

Groundwater Analysis Report
Linear model: groundwater level ~ rainfall. R² = 0.49.
“Rainfall is the dominant control on groundwater levels.”


Now look at the diagnostic plots…


[15 min] Show diagnostic plots with a clear seasonal pattern in the residuals. There’s a time-lag and seasonal cycle the model isn’t capturing.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What’s wrong?


Figure 1

w08-residuals.R


The residuals show a seasonal pattern — the model is missing a time-dependent structure
R² = 0.49 means 51% of the variation is unexplained
“Dominant” is a stretch when your model misses more than it captures



Key question: what is the model not capturing? (Seasonal recharge, time lag between rainfall and groundwater response, temperature effects on evapotranspiration.)

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 1: Overfitting
A model that fits the training data perfectly but fails on new data.
It’s memorised the noise.


[25 min block] Three failures — each a different form of hubris. Demo the polynomial overfitting live.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Demo: polynomial degree 15

🖥️ Live demo

Fit a degree-15 polynomial to 20 data points. It goes through every point but oscillates wildly between them.
Compare to the straight line: fits worse, predicts better.


More complex ≠ more useful.



Live-code: geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 15)) vs y ~ x on the same plot. The visual contrast is striking.
The next slide is the same contrast, pre-rendered — use it as the fallback if WebR misbehaves, and leave it up while they discuss.

title: Models and their limits
text:
What that looks like


Figure 2

w08-overfitting.R



Both R² values are read off the fitted models. “Fits worse, predicts better” is arithmetic here, not rhetoric.
Ask for a prediction at x = 11 from each model. One of them has an answer; the other has left the building.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 2: Extrapolation
A model that works within the observed range but breaks down outside it.

Example: UK solar capacity has grown roughly exponentially since 2010. Extrapolate to 2050 → solar exceeds the entire UK grid.








Figure 3






w08-extrapolation.R



What’s the model not capturing?
Planning constraints, grid limits, diminishing suitable sites.

title: Models and their limits
text:
HolmesCo’s extrapolation


HolmesCo
“Geological Solutions Since 2019”

“Our linear trend in groundwater decline predicts the aquifer will be empty by 2028.”
They didn’t account for seasonal recharge or the fact that the decline was caused by temporary pumping.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Failure 3: Blind spots
Things the model structurally cannot represent.


A single-turbine power curve has no term for wake interference → overpredicts wind farm output by 10–20%
A carbon accounting model that counts biomass as zero structurally cannot see the emissions it ignores




You can only fix a blind spot if you know it’s there.

title: Models and their limits
text: The new refrain

title: Models and their limits
text:
“What is the model not capturing?”
Overfitting: too much faith in your data.
Extrapolation: too much faith in your model.
Blind spots: too much faith in your framework.


These are three forms of the same mistake: confusing the map for the territory. Each is a different flavour of hubris.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Write one sentence

“In my project, the biggest thing my analysis might be missing is…”



[5 min] Quick written reflection. Students keep this for their reports.

title: Models and their limits
text:
Key points

A model is a simplification — powerful, but limited
Always check the diagnostics: residuals don’t lie
Three failures: overfitting, extrapolation, blind spots
Always ask: “What is my model not capturing?”
